briefing:
The headline Airfare Price Index (APIx) registered at 101.65 for the target observation period of September 7, 2026, marking a aggregate price increase of 1.65% over base levels across monitored domestic trunk corridors. Overall, the market exhibits a moderate inflationary trend driven primarily by strong dynamic pricing in regional non-stop markets and near-term booking demand. Sectoral performance indicates that price expansion was led by the Calcutta – Bombay corridor, which recorded a route-level APIx of 103.16 (+3.16%), followed by Delhi – Bengaluru at 102.23 (+2.23%). Conversely, the heavily weighted Delhi – Bombay route remained virtually unchanged relative to base medians, printing a route-level APIx of 100.07 (+0.07%) and acting as a stabilizing anchor for the broader macro index.

A granular evaluation of advance booking windows reveals that index gains were concentrated at opposite ends of the booking curve. The growth in the Calcutta – Bombay route was heavily propelled by a 29.98% surge in the short-notice T+1 window—where median target prices surged from ₹9,584 to ₹12,457—alongside a 15.37% rise in the T+45 window to ₹14,899.50. On the Delhi – Bengaluru route, index upward pressure stemmed predominantly from the T+7 window, which surged 16.29% to a target median of ₹10,011.50 (weighted at 30%), effectively overriding moderate price declines in the intermediate T+15 (-6.32%) and T+30 (-2.93%) windows. Meanwhile, the Delhi – Bombay route demonstrated balanced dynamics: modest yield increases in the T+1 (+5.67%), T+7 (+2.46%), and T+45 (+5.01%) windows were offset by soft pricing across T+15 (-3.52%) and T+30 (-3.23%) departures.

Analysis of individual flight itineraries from the scraped dataset reveals significant structural fare dispersion and carrier-level pricing strategies. Notably, secondary airport infrastructure is actively expanding market segmentation; for instance, on the Delhi – Bombay T+7 departure, Akasa Air offered floor fares at ₹5,382 out of Jewar (DXN), markedly undercutting the primary Delhi (DEL) to Mumbai (BOM) non-stop standard fare of ₹6,530. A similar phenomenon appears in Navi Mumbai (NMI) and Ghaziabad/Hindon (HDO) routing options across multiple time horizons. Wide price spreads were also observed on the Calcutta – Bombay T+45 corridor, where full-service carriers pushed upper-tail fares up to ₹17,389 for non-stop departures, pulling median prices upward despite budget carriers listing one-stop options around ₹10,081. Conversely, selective carrier interventions—such as Air India’s promotional deal fares at ₹7,999 on Delhi – Bengaluru at T+7—temporarily flattened floor pricing on specific legs.

Looking forward, the persistence of elevated near-term (T+1) dynamic pricing alongside firm advance (T+45) bookings points to resilient underlying domestic travel demand, presenting mild upside risks to the transport and services components of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). However, the rising market share and lower base fares from peripheral airport hubs (DXN, NMI, HDO) appear to be absorbing peak capacity pressures and capping broader systemic inflation across main trunk lines. Monetary policy oversight should remain watchful of potential second-round pass-through effects into core inflation if near-term travel demand tightens further into upcoming high-traffic seasonal cycles, while statistical monitoring should continue refining route-weight adjustments to account for shifting multi-airport metropolitan travel patterns.
